title: Six Rooms Again
bigQuestion: How can sorting martial arts into families help a historian compare them without claiming that one is better?

story.title: Six Objects on a Shelf
story.kicker: Each object on the shelf points to a different room and a different set of records.
paragraphs: A museum storage shelf holds six objects with paper tags. There is a leather belt harness from Iceland and a pair of laced French boxing shoes. There is a bamboo practice sword from Japan and a printed booklet of a simplified taijiquan routine from Beijing, dated 1956.

The last two objects are a polished stick from Trinidad and a training manual in Hebrew from Israel. A curator must file them. One tag asks for a family name: grappling, striking, armed as sport, flowing practice, diaspora, or modern mix.

The curator notices that the tags do not rank the objects. A grappling harness is not higher than a stick. Each category only groups things that share a trait, such as a weapon, a contest, or a history of travel. Some objects could fit under two tags at once.

Scholars of martial arts face the same filing problem. Japanese federations, American authors and UNESCO have each drawn up lists and families. Every list was made by a real body, in a real year, for its own purpose. Reading who made a list is the first step in using it well.
story.think: Why might one object fit under two tags, and what does that tell you about categories?

lessons.title: Nine Arts, One Association
lessons.mainIdea: The Japanese Budo Association, founded in 1977, groups nine modern budo arts, so its list is a record of one body's choices.
reading: In 1977 nine Japanese federations joined with the Nippon Budokan to form the *Japanese Budo Association*. The nine arts were judo, kendo, kyudo, sumo, karatedo, aikido, shorinji kempo, naginata and jukendo. Kyudo is Japanese archery. Naginata uses a long curved blade on a pole, and jukendo uses a wooden rifle with a blunt bayonet.

The Nippon Budokan is the hall in Tokyo built for judo at the 1964 Olympic Games. It became the home of the new association. In 1987 the association issued the *Budo Charter*, a short document of principles. The charter describes budo as a way of building character, respect and self-discipline, in the words of its authors.

The list is a *category*, a group drawn around shared traits. Its borders were set by people. Many Japanese arts older than 1868 are not on it, and neither is kickboxing. The list tells a historian which modern federations worked together in Japan after 1977. It does not say those nine arts are better than others.

words.d: a body formed in 1977 by nine Japanese budo federations and the Nippon Budokan
a 1987 statement of principles for modern budo issued by the Japanese Budo Association
a group that people draw around things sharing a trait
a modern Japanese budo art practiced with a wooden rifle and bayonet

look.prompt: What might explain why some arts practiced in Japan are on this list and others are not?

check.why: Nine federations and the Nippon Budokan formed the association in 1977.

check.q: What is kyudo?
check.why: The reading explains that kyudo is Japanese archery.

choices: A ranking from best to worst
A group drawn around shared traits
A law passed by a parliament

lessons.title: Old Schools and New Budo
lessons.mainIdea: Japanese historians often separate koryu, schools founded before 1868, from gendai budo, arts shaped in modern Japan, but the line is a tool.
reading: In Japan the word *koryu* means old school or old stream. It usually names a martial tradition founded before the Meiji Restoration of 1868. Many koryu passed teaching through one family or one licensed line. They kept written scrolls that listed the school's founder and its later heads.

The word *gendai budo* means modern budo. It names arts organized after 1868, such as judo from 1882, kendo's national rules, aikido and karatedo. Gendai budo usually has open membership, printed rules and national federations. Many of these arts also hold public contests with referees.

The American author Donn F. Draeger wrote three books on this split: *Classical Bujutsu* and *Classical Budo* in 1973 and *Modern Bujutsu and Budo* in 1974. He used 1868 as a working border. Later historians noted that many koryu kept changing after 1868 and that modern arts borrowed from old ones. The border helps sort records; it does not settle which art is more genuine.

words.d: a Japanese martial tradition, usually one founded before 1868; literally old school or old stream
modern budo; Japanese arts organized after 1868 with open membership and printed rules
the 1868 change that returned rule to the Japanese emperor and began rapid modernization

look.title: A Working Border in Three Books
look.text: Draeger divided Japanese fighting arts by period. Classical arts came from the age of the warrior class before 1868. Modern arts grew after 1868, when Japan built schools, an army of conscripts and national sport bodies.
look.cite: Donn F. Draeger, The Martial Arts and Ways of Japan series, Classical Bujutsu (1973), Classical Budo (1973), Modern Bujutsu and Budo (1974)
look.prompt: Why might a single year work well as a border for some records and poorly for others?

check.q: What does koryu mean?
check.why: Koryu means old school or old stream and usually names a tradition founded before 1868.

check.q: Which year did Draeger use as a working border?
check.why: Draeger split classical and modern arts at 1868, the Meiji Restoration.

check.q: What did later historians point out about the 1868 border?
choices: Old schools kept changing and new arts borrowed from them
check.why: Historians noted change after 1868 and borrowing between old and new arts.

lessons.title: A Heritage List as a Map
lessons.mainIdea: UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage has named several martial practices since 2010, each nominated by a state for its own reasons.
reading: UNESCO adopted a Convention for the Safeguarding of the *Intangible Cultural Heritage* in 2003. Intangible heritage means living practices such as songs, crafts, festivals and games, not buildings. A state nominates a practice, and a UNESCO committee decides whether to inscribe it on a list.

Turkey's Kırkpınar oil wrestling festival and Iran's Pahlevani and zoorkhanei rituals were inscribed in 2010. South Korea's taekkyeon followed in 2011, Brazil's capoeira circle in 2014, and Korean ssireum in 2018. That ssireum listing was the first joint nomination by North and South Korea. Taijiquan from China joined in 2020.

The list mixes wrestling, ritual exercise, music and flowing routines. What joins them is a *nomination*, a formal request by a government. Governments choose what to nominate for reasons of pride, tourism and protection. A historian reads the list as a record of states naming their heritage, not as a ranking of arts.

words.d: living practices such as songs, games and rituals that UNESCO lists for protection
a formal request by a state asking UNESCO to list a practice
Korean wrestling, listed by UNESCO in 2018 after a joint nomination by both Koreas

look.title: Martial Practices on UNESCO's List
look.cite: UNESCO, Lists of Intangible Cultural Heritage, inscription records
look.prompt: Which listings came in the same year, and what kinds of practice do the six entries include?

check.q: What makes heritage intangible?
choices: It is a living practice such as a game or song
check.why: Intangible heritage means living practices, not buildings or objects.

check.q: Which listing was the first joint nomination by North and South Korea?
check.why: Ssireum, listed in 2018, was the first joint nomination by both Koreas.

check.q: Who nominates a practice for the list?
check.why: A state makes the formal nomination; a UNESCO committee decides.

lessons.title: Glima in Stockholm
lessons.mainIdea: Icelandic glima, a belt wrestling tradition, was shown to the world as a demonstration at the 1912 Stockholm Olympics.
reading: *Glima* is the traditional wrestling of Iceland. Wrestlers wear a leather belt harness around the waist and thighs, and they hold it during a bout. Icelandic sagas written down in the 1200s and 1300s describe men wrestling at gatherings. Glima is often named as Iceland's national sport.

At the 1912 Olympic Games in Stockholm, Icelandic wrestlers performed glima as a *demonstration*. A demonstration event is shown at the Games but awards no official Olympic medals. Iceland was then still under the Danish crown. Showing glima in Stockholm let Icelanders present a sport of their own to a world audience.

Glima belongs to the grappling family, the arts where contestants seize and control each other rather than strike. The family is very old and very wide. It also holds Greek wrestling, Japanese sumo, Mongolian bökh and Swiss schwingen. Each kept its own clothing, ring and rules, so the family name groups them without merging them.

words.d: the traditional belt wrestling of Iceland
an event shown at the Olympic Games that awards no official medals
a family of arts in which contestants seize and control each other rather than strike

look.title: A Harness on a Hook
look.text: A worn leather harness hangs on a hook in Reykjavík. It has a wide band for the waist and two loops for the thighs. A tag says it was used in glima contests. Beside it hangs a smooth wrestling singlet from an American high school, with nothing for an opponent to grip.
look.prompt: What can the two garments tell you about how the rules of each contest differ, without describing any hold?

check.why: Glima is the traditional belt wrestling of Iceland.

check.q: What was glima's role at the 1912 Olympics?
choices: A demonstration with no official medals
check.why: Icelanders showed glima as a demonstration at Stockholm in 1912.

check.q: Which art is in the grappling family, as the reading lists it?
check.why: The reading names schwingen with sumo, bökh and Greek wrestling as grappling arts.

lessons.title: Savate in Paris
lessons.mainIdea: Savate, or boxe française, grew in Paris in the 1800s when French teachers joined foot fighting with English boxing into a rule-bound sport.
reading: In the early 1800s, *savate* was a street fighting style in Paris and the port of Marseille. Its name comes from an old French word for a worn shoe. Michel Casseux, a Paris teacher, opened a training room for it in the 1820s. Police and polite society often saw savate as the fighting of the poor.

Charles Lecour, a pupil of Casseux, studied English boxing in the 1830s. He joined English punching with French kicking and taught the blend in his salle, or training hall. The result came to be called *boxe française*, French boxing. Wealthy Parisians began to attend Lecour's salle.

Late in the century, Joseph Charlemont and his son Charles ran a well-known Paris salle and wrote books on the sport. Their work gave boxe française printed rules and a teaching system. Savate belongs to the striking family, which also holds boxing, Muay Thai and karate. Like those arts, it moved from street or village use to a salle with rules.

words.d: a French fighting sport with kicks and punches; also called boxe française
French boxing; the name for savate after teachers blended it with English boxing
French for hall; a training room for fencing or French boxing
a family of arts in which contestants score with blows, such as boxing and karate

look.title: Two Rooms in One City
look.text: Paris, 1830s. In one district, dock workers settle quarrels in the street with kicks, and police write reports. Across the river, Charles Lecour's salle has a fee, a teacher, a timetable and polished shoes. Wealthy students come there after work.
look.prompt: How did moving savate into a paid salle change who practiced it and how others saw it?

choices: An old French word for a worn shoe
check.why: Savate comes from an old French word for a worn shoe.

check.q: What did Charles Lecour blend with French kicking?
check.why: Lecour studied English boxing in the 1830s and joined it with French kicking.

check.q: What did the Charlemonts add to boxe française?
choices: Printed rules and a teaching system in their books
check.why: Joseph and Charles Charlemont wrote books that gave the sport printed rules and a teaching system.

lessons.title: Kickboxing Gets a Name
lessons.mainIdea: The word kickboxing was coined in Japan in the mid-1960s for a new ring sport drawn from Muay Thai, karate and boxing.
reading: In the early 1960s, Thai boxers and Japanese karate fighters met in bouts in Japan and Thailand. The Japanese promoter Noguchi Osamu watched these meetings. In the mid-1960s he organized a new ring sport and gave it the English name *kickboxing*. Japanese television soon broadcast kickboxing cards, and the sport grew popular in Japan.

Kickboxing was a *hybrid*, a sport built from parts of several older arts. It kept the gloves and rounds of Western boxing. It borrowed scoring and kicks from Muay Thai and fighters from karate schools. Its rule books were new, and so were its title belts and weight classes.

In 1993 a Japanese karate leader, Ishii Kazuyoshi, founded the K-1 promotion in Japan. K-1 held kickboxing tournaments with fighters from many countries. Kickboxing shows how a modern mix grows: promoters, broadcasters and rule writers join pieces of older arts into a new *promotion*. The sport's history can be read in its founding years and its companies.

words.d: a ring sport named in Japan in the 1960s that joins boxing gloves and rounds with kicks
something built by joining parts of several older things
a company that organizes and sells public fight events

look.title: Three Parents on One Poster
look.text: A Tokyo fight poster from the late 1960s shows two gloved fighters under the English word kickboxing. The small print lists a television channel, a promoter's name and three rounds per bout. One fighter is described as a karate man, the other as a Thai boxer.
look.prompt: Which details on the poster point to boxing, which to karate, and which to Muay Thai?

check.q: Who gave the new Japanese ring sport the name kickboxing?
check.why: The promoter Noguchi Osamu organized and named kickboxing in the mid-1960s.

check.q: What is a hybrid, as the reading uses the word?
choices: Something built from parts of older things
check.why: A hybrid is built by joining parts of several older things, as kickboxing did.

check.q: What was K-1, founded in 1993?
check.why: Ishii Kazuyoshi founded K-1 in 1993 to hold kickboxing tournaments.

lessons.title: Bamboo and Armor
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1700s, Japanese sword schools adopted bamboo swords and padded armor, which later let kendo become a contest sport.
reading: Early Japanese sword schools trained mostly with wooden swords in set, paired routines. In the 1700s, teachers in the Jikishinkage-ryū and Ittō-ryū lines are credited with spreading protective armor and bamboo swords. The *shinai* is a practice sword made of four bamboo staves bound with leather. The armor, called *bogu*, covers the head, body and hands.

The new gear allowed full-speed contests with less risk of injury. By the early 1800s, large sword training halls in Edo, today's Tokyo, held such contests. After 1868 the sword lost its place in daily life, and the contests became public shows called gekiken. Around 1920 the Dai Nippon Butoku Kai adopted the name kendo, the way of the sword.

Kendo belongs to the armed-as-sport family. In these arts, a weapon has been made safe enough to score with. Olympic fencing, sport arnis and kendo all share this trait. In each, a change in equipment came before a change in rules, and the rules then shaped how the sport was judged.

words.d: a kendo practice sword made of four bamboo staves bound with leather
kendo armor covering the head, body and hands
a family of arts in which a weapon has been made safe enough to score with in contests

look.title: Wood, Then Bamboo
look.text: Two practice swords lie side by side. One is solid oak, heavy, used for set routines between partners who stop short of contact. The other is four bamboo staves tied with leather cord, light, with a leather cap on the tip. A padded helmet sits next to it.
look.prompt: Why would the bamboo sword and helmet make scored contests possible where the oak sword did not?

check.q: What is a shinai made of?
choices: Four bamboo staves bound with leather
check.why: A shinai is four bamboo staves bound with leather.

check.q: When did the Dai Nippon Butoku Kai adopt the name kendo?
check.why: The Butoku Kai adopted the name kendo around 1920.

check.q: What trait joins the armed-as-sport family?
choices: A weapon made safe enough to score with
check.why: Arts in this family made a weapon safe enough for scored contests.

lessons.title: Taijiquan in a Beijing Park
lessons.mainIdea: Taijiquan spread from Chen Village to Beijing in the 1800s, and a 1956 simplified routine made it a mass health practice in China.
reading: Yang Luchan, who lived from 1799 to 1872, studied taijiquan with the Chen family in Henan Province. He later taught in Beijing, the capital of the Qing dynasty. His students included men of the Manchu banner households. The Yang family line he began became one of the most practiced forms of taijiquan in the world.

In 1956 China's national sports commission published a *simplified* taijiquan routine of 24 movements. It was drawn from Yang-style forms and was shorter than older family routines. The goal was a practice that millions of people could learn for health. Group practice in parks and squares at dawn became a familiar sight in Chinese cities.

Taijiquan is often placed in a flowing family: *solo forms* done slowly, often without a partner or opponent. Many practitioners describe it as exercise, health care and moving meditation. Contest events also exist, such as judged taijiquan routines in modern wushu. So the same art can be sorted into more than one family, depending on the room.

words.d: made shorter and easier; the 1956 taijiquan routine had 24 movements
a set routine practiced by one person, without a partner
a teacher (1799–1872) who learned taijiquan in Chen Village and taught it in Beijing

look.title: Dawn in a Square
look.text: Six in the morning in a Beijing park. Forty retired workers move slowly in rows while a small speaker plays music. A leader faces them. Nobody keeps score. Nearby, a printed poster names the 24-movement routine and the year 1956.
look.prompt: Which family would you file this scene under, and what could make you file the same art somewhere else?

check.why: Yang Luchan taught in Beijing, the Qing capital.

check.q: How many movements did the 1956 simplified routine have?
check.why: The 1956 routine from China's sports commission had 24 movements.

check.q: Why can taijiquan fit more than one family?
choices: It is practiced as health exercise and also judged in wushu contests
It is a kind of wrestling
check.why: Taijiquan is practiced as flowing health exercise and also appears as judged routines in wushu.

lessons.title: Aikido Without Contests
lessons.mainIdea: Ueshiba Morihei's aikido, named in 1942, was organized by the Aikikai largely without competitions, while a later branch added them.
reading: Ueshiba Morihei, who lived from 1883 to 1969, studied Daitō-ryū jujutsu under Takeda Sōkaku from 1915. In 1931 he opened a training hall in Tokyo called the Kobukan. The name *aikido* came into official use in 1942. After the war, in 1948, Japan's government approved the *Aikikai* as a foundation to run the art.

The Aikikai chose not to hold contests. Its members practice in pairs and test for ranks before examiners instead of winners and losers. Ueshiba described aikido in spiritual and ethical terms, as a way of harmony. Those are his words and beliefs, and many Aikikai schools teach them as part of the art.

Not every aikido teacher agreed. Tomiki Kenji, a judo and aikido teacher, developed an aikido branch that includes competition. So aikido itself has more than one room. A family label such as flowing practice fits one branch well and the other less well.

words.d: a Japanese art founded by Ueshiba Morihei; the name came into official use in 1942
the foundation approved in 1948 to run Ueshiba's aikido, which holds no contests
a legally recognized body set up to carry on a purpose, such as teaching an art

check.why: Ueshiba studied Daitō-ryū jujutsu under Takeda Sōkaku from 1915.

check.why: Aikikai members test for ranks before examiners instead of contests.

lessons.title: Kalinda in Trinidad
lessons.mainIdea: Kalinda stick fighting in Trinidad grew among Africans and their descendants, and colonial laws in the 1880s tried to restrict it.
reading: *Kalinda* is a stick-fighting tradition of Trinidad in the Caribbean. It grew among enslaved Africans and their descendants on the island. Fighters, called *batonniers*, meet in a ring while drummers and singers perform. The songs, called kalinda songs, are part of the event, not an extra.

Britain ended slavery in its colonies by law in 1834, with full freedom in 1838. Freed people in Trinidad made Carnival their own, including the night festival of Canboulay. In 1881 police in Port of Spain tried to stop the Canboulay procession, and fighting broke out. In 1884 the colonial government passed a law that restricted drumming and the gatherings of stick-fighting bands.

Kalinda survived in villages and at Carnival. Trinidad and Tobago became independent in 1962, and stick-fighting contests still appear in its Carnival season. Kalinda belongs to the *diaspora* family: arts carried or rebuilt by people scattered from a homeland. Afro-Brazilian capoeira, with its music and ring, shows a similar history of law and survival.

words.d: an Afro-Trinidadian stick-fighting tradition with drumming and song
a stick fighter in Trinidad's kalinda tradition
people scattered from a homeland, and the culture they carry or rebuild
a night Carnival procession in Trinidad; police tried to stop it in 1881

look.title: Two Laws Against Two Arts
look.text: Brazil, 1890: a penal code names capoeira a crime. Trinidad, 1884: a colonial law restricts drumming and stick-fighting bands. Both arts were practiced by people of African descent. Both came with music. Both survived and are now shown as national heritage.
look.prompt: What does the pattern in these two laws suggest about why governments targeted these arts?

lessons.title: Krav Maga in Israel
lessons.mainIdea: Imi Lichtenfeld built krav maga, a modern mixed self-defense system, for Jewish defense groups and then the Israel Defense Forces.
reading: Imi Lichtenfeld, who lived from 1910 to 1998, grew up in Bratislava, then in Czechoslovakia. He competed in boxing, wrestling and gymnastics. In the 1930s he helped organize Jewish young people to defend their neighborhoods against antisemitic gangs. He left Europe in 1940 and reached Mandatory Palestine, then under British rule, in the early 1940s.

There he trained fighters of the Haganah, a Jewish defense force. After Israel became a state in 1948, he became chief instructor of physical fitness and *krav maga* for the Israel Defense Forces. The Hebrew name means contact combat. He retired from the army in 1964 and then opened civilian schools.

Krav maga is a *modern mix*: a system built in the twentieth century from boxing, wrestling and other sources, with no contest code. Its main room was a military one, not a stadium. Sambo in the Soviet Union and kickboxing in Japan are other modern mixes. Each was shaped by a specific institution, in a specific decade, for a specific purpose.

words.d: a self-defense system built by Imi Lichtenfeld; the Hebrew name means contact combat
a system built in modern times from several older arts
a Jewish defense force in Mandatory Palestine before Israel became a state in 1948

look.title: Three Modern Mixes, Three Owners
look.text: Kickboxing: a Japanese promoter and television, 1960s. Sambo: Soviet sports and army bodies, 1930s. Krav maga: the Israel Defense Forces, after 1948. Each borrowed from older arts. Each served the body that shaped it.
look.prompt: How did the institution behind each mix shape whether it kept a contest code?

check.why: Krav maga means contact combat in Hebrew.

check.q: Which institution was krav maga's main room after 1948?
check.why: Lichtenfeld was chief instructor of krav maga for the Israel Defense Forces.

check.q: Where did Imi Lichtenfeld grow up?
